notes.meaning: The Philistine army gathered at Aphek to prepare for war against Israel. King Saul and his soldiers set up their camp further north by a large water spring near Jezreel. This set the stage for Saul's final, tragic battle against his long-time enemies.

The Philistine rulers marched their troops forward in organized units of hundreds and thousands. David and his six hundred men marched at the very rear as the personal bodyguard of King Achish of Gath. This placed David in a terrible spot, because marching with Philistines meant being expected to fight against his own people.

When the other Philistine rulers saw David's troops, they asked why these Hebrews were present in their battle line. Achish defended David, explaining that David had left Saul long ago and had served him faithfully without any wrongdoing. Achish fully trusted David, unaware that David had secretly remained loyal to Israel all along.

The other commanders were furious and demanded that Achish send David back to his assigned town of Ziklag. They feared that David would turn on them during the clash and kill Philistine soldiers to win back King Saul's favor. Through their anger and suspicion, God stepped in to rescue David from an impossible choice.

The commanders quoted the famous song the women of Israel had sung to celebrate David's past victories over the Philistines. They remembered how deadly David had been to their people and refused to trust him now. Even among his enemies, David's past service to God and his nation could not be forgotten.

Achish summoned David and swore an oath using the name of the Lord, declaring that he considered David upright and blameless. Even so, Achish explained that the other Philistine rulers refused to let him march with them. Achish valued David's service, but he was forced to yield to the decision of his fellow leaders.

Achish urged David to turn back quietly and go home in peace to avoid angering the Philistine lords any further. Although Achish spoke with regret, his order was an answer to prayer for David. God used the distrust of David's enemies to open an honorable way of escape.

David protested his innocence and asked what he had done to be barred from fighting the king's enemies. On the surface, David acted deeply offended, even though he was surely relieved not to fight his own countrymen. His words were carefully phrased so that 'my lord the king' could secretly refer to Saul rather than Achish.

Achish repeated his praise, telling David that he viewed him as noble and trustworthy as an angel of God. Even so, he insisted that the Philistine commanders had made a final ruling against David joining the battle. As a king whose power was checked by other rulers, Achish had no choice but to follow their demands.

Achish instructed David and his men to get up early the next morning and leave as soon as it was light. By calling David's soldiers 'your master's servants,' Achish echoed the Philistine lords' view that these men were still Saul's subjects. Leaving at first light allowed them to depart safely without facing hostility from the rest of the army.

David and his men set out at dawn to return toward Philistine territory, while the Philistine army moved ahead toward Jezreel. David was spared from fighting Israel, and leaving early allowed him to reach his home town of Ziklag just in time to face another crisis. God's unseen care protected David even when he had put himself in grave danger.
